video_title: How China Keeps Winning by Doing Nothing
transcript: The United States and Israel initiated a major war in the Middle East against Iran. And the biggest winner of this war isn't going to be any of them. It's going to be China instead. Back at the end of February, when the US and Israel decided to launch this war, they did so with the expectation that the exact opposite outcome would follow with China becoming severely weakened and humbled. If the staunchly anti-Western regime in Iran were toppled by the war, then China would lose a major source of its discounted oil. Because of the crippling financial sanctions placed on Iran by the West, Iran has always had very few countries actually willing to purchase their oil at scale other than China, which has enabled China to buy up Iranian oil at a steep discount off of its usual market value. Roughly 13% of all of China's oil imports were likely coming cheaply from Iran immediately before the war began. And so cutting that supply off would have placed even further pressure on China following the US abduction of Nicholas Maduro in Venezuela that took place just a few weeks beforehand. Similar to Iran, crippling Western financial sanctions placed on Maduro's regime in Venezuela had meant that there were very few countries willing to purchase Venezuelan oil other than China, which meant that China could apply leverage on Venezuela to purchase their oil for a steep discount. Roughly 3% of China's total oil imports were similarly coming cheaply from Venezuela, which the US was able to largely sever and redirect to itself after they seized Maduro and changed the country's leadership through a rapid military raid. Were the US to manage to topple the Iranian regime and reroute their oil exports as well, China would have become severed from two of its largest sources of cheap discounted oil, representing about 16% of its usual total imports that would have had to have been replaced from somewhere else. And even better from Washington's perspective, China would have become exposed as a weak bystander of global events that was unable or unwilling to defend friendly regimes in both Venezuela and Iran alike. The US would be able to clearly display that its superpower strength still remained the dominant force in [music] the world, while China would be shown as a fair weather friend and a weaker power that could not be relied upon to help resist Washington. Or so Washington's theory of victory went when they decided to start the war. But over the months since then, all of those initial American assumptions about how the war would negatively affect China have proven to have been disastrously wrong. The meme of China doing nothing and winning right now does have some element of truth behind it. But that meme betrays the fact that China is actually doing a lot behind the scenes to counter whatever America is throwing [music] at it. It's been well understood in China for decades now that one of the country's greatest vulnerabilities is its lack of oil within their own borders. China still to this day relies on imports from abroad to meet about 70% of its total oil consumption. About half of which also still comes from around the Persian Gulf. Thus, if you eliminate China's oil imports from the Persian Gulf, you eliminate about 35% of the source of China's total oil [music] consumption, which is exactly the scenario that happened when Iran enforced a total closure the straight of Hormos during the war. One would logically assume that the sudden and immediate loss of roughly 35% of China's usual oil supply would have tripled the Chinese economy. But that didn't actually ever happen because China has spent decades diligently preparing for a scenario that is almost exactly identical to this. China has always been very paranoid about what it calls its Malaa dilemma. The fact that the overwhelming majority of its critical oil imports flow through the narrow straight of Malaa that during wartime could become easily blockaded by the US Navy. Defending and countering against that mala dilemma has been at the core of Chinese foreign policy for decades now. But little did Beijing expect that their preparations for that would also end up coming in handy for when Iran shut down the straight of war muz as well. To prepare for a possible American blockade of their seaborn oil imports during a war over Taiwan, China has pursued a multi-pronged strategy of diversifying their sources of oil imports, building up their stockpiles of oil, and destroying their own domestic demand for oil. Let's go through these points one by one. First, China spent decades quietly building up what has become the world's largest national strategic reserve of oil. On paper, China's strategic reserve of oil might appear to be lower than America's. By December of 2025, according to the Energy Information Administration or EIA, the Chinese government officially held 359 million barrels of oil in reserve, while the US government officially held 413 million barrels in reserve. However, most of the commercial inventories of oil in China that are technically outside of the official strategic reserve are also held by Chinese stateowned oil companies, which blurs the line between the country's government- held and commercial held reserves. While in the US, the country's commercially held inventories of oil are fully separate from the government's reserves. Thus, by the end of 2025, the Chinese government had effectively established a strategic reserve of oil that was more than three times the size of America's. It was buoied by massive purchases of oil by the Chinese throughout 2025 that filled up their stock piles when the price of oil was comparatively lower. And it was enough to fully last 100% of China's usual oil consumption for more than 100 days without any additional imports or societal changes at all. By comparison, the US strategic reserve only held enough at the start of 2026 to fully provide for 100% of America's usual oil consumption for a mere 20 days, 1/5 as long as China's. In addition to that, China's worked hard over the past several years to radically diversify the sources of oil they import to reduce their dependencies on any single given geographic location. While about half of China's oil imports come from around the Persian Gulf through the straight of Arm Buzz, that ratio was much lower for China than just about every other nation in East Asia. Japan relied on about 93% of its oil imports from the Persian Gulf. South Korea relied on the region for about 70% of theirs, while Taiwan relied on it for about 58% of theirs. So comparatively to the rest of the major economies of East Asia, China was relatively less exposed to disruption in the straight of Hormuz and they had a much much larger stockpile of oil held in reserve to get them through any crisis as well. And on top of those two factors, [music] China has also spent years crafting a national energy strategy to reduce their economic dependence on oil as a resource altogether as well, which ironically has made heavy use of both coal and renewable technologies alike. While China doesn't really have a lot of oil within their own borders, they do have a ton of coal. Like to the point where China has the third largest proven reserves of coal in the world, just behind Russia. Thus, China still relies on its own huge domestic reserves of coal that can't be blockaded from abroad to provide for a significant amount of their own energy and electricity demand. Roughly 56% of China's total energy supply still comes from burning coal compared to only 18% from oil and just 9% from natural gas. And China's electricity production is even more lopsided in coal's favor with 60% of the nation's electricity generated through coal compared to only 3% from oil and gas combined. And most of the rest comes through China's massive investments into renewable and nuclear energy technologies. China installed almost half of the entire world's solar and wind energy capacity in 2024. [music] Solar and wind accounted for 22% of China's total energy needs in 2022. and they plan [music] to increase that share even further to 30% by 2030. At the same time, China is doubling down on their nuclear energy as well. In 2024, 4.5% of China's electricity came from nuclear power, but they're planning on increasing that share up to 10% by 2035. [music] Overall, wind, solar, and nuclear energy contributed to more than 22% of China's electricity generation in 2024. About another 13% came from hydropower and another 60% came from coal. Meaning that China was already almost completely independent from oil and gas to keep their electricity going. By comparison, South Korea still relies on imported oil and gas to power 29% of their own electricity. Japan for 34% of theirs and Taiwan for a whopping 44% of theirs. In most economies, rising oil prices most usually affects consumers at the fuel pump when they go to fill up their cars with gasoline. But since the early 2000s, in order to reduce their dependence on foreign oil even further and to shield more of their population from oil supply crunches, China's pursued a relentless strategy of adopting as many EVs in the country as possible. By 2024, roughly 11% of all the passenger vehicles on the road in China were EVs. a bit behind countries like Denmark and Sweden, but well ahead of any of their regional rivals like South Korea and the United States with only a 3% share of EVs on their roads, or Japan with just a 1% share of EVs on their roads. All of this combined, from China's massive stockpiles of oil to its almost zero use of oil for electricity generation and to its high adoption rate of EVs on the road meant that China was well prepared to weather through a massive oil supply shock that came when Iran began blocking the straight of muzz. China was therefore able to cut back on their imported oil purchases during the war by approximately 4 million barrels per day, equivalent to double the oil consumption rate of Germany with relatively minimal effects on their society and economy for several months. China cut down on their oil purchases by so much during the war that it effectively set a cap on how high the global price of oil would actually go up to. Had China not done that, the price for everyone around the world would have gotten much, much much worse, and it's established a lot of leverage over the United States in doing so. Were China to begin buying up oil again now at its usual pace with Hormuz still closed, it would dramatically jack the price of oil back up beyond even the highest points it has reached so far and exacerbate inflation in the US and everywhere else in the world too, which the US obviously doesn't want and which China can use as leverage right now to gain concessions out of the US. All of these strategies were adopted by China to help the nation get through a US blockade of their oil imports in the Balaca Strait. But as it turned out, they worked just as well to get through an Iranian blockade of their oil imports through the straight of Hormuz, too. Moreover, the way that the war and the closure of Hormuz spiked global oil prices has also proven to be a massive advertisement to other countries for the great energy technologies that China currently dominates the manufacturing of. Governments around the world were suddenly reminded of how overdependency on a highly volatile energy resource like oil can rapidly increase nationwide inflation when it spikes in price due to unforeseen events. While demand for alternative green energy technologies like solar panels, wind turbines, EVs, and batteries were already growing even beforehand anyway. [music] And that demand has only increased since the war began. And since the US is the world's largest oil producer and China is the world's largest clean energy hardware producer, this shift is obviously going to be to China's benefit and America's detriment. Devoid of hardly any oil resources in their own territory, China has been betting big on green energy alternatives instead for decades. Not just out of a desire to move away from fossil fuels for climate reasons, but also out of raw geopolitical calculus and energy self-sufficiency. As early as 2000, China understood that in order to defeat the western world of the automotive industry, it needed to skip over gasoline powered internal combustion engine vehicles directly to EVs. Today, major Chinese EV manufacturing companies like BYD, Gily, Xpang, and others control an overwhelming 70% of the global production of EVs, which also means that China dominates the global production of the critical lithium ion batteries that power EVs as well. 89% of global lithium-ion battery capacity is currently manufactured in China [music] today. And their dominance in green energy hardware doesn't stop there. China has similarly bet big on solar panels since 2000 as well. And today they produce approximately 80% of the world's supply of solar panels. Ever concerned with their own domestic green energy industries that they want to protect, both the US and EU have long maintained high tariffs on Chinese technology to block their entry into their markets. The US currently maintains a steep 100% tariff on Chinese EVs and a 50% tariff on Chinese solar panels, while the EU maintains a lower but still fairly high tariff of 35% on Chinese EVs as well. But the rest of the world beyond America and Europe have been buying [music] up Chinese green energy tech at record paces since the war with Iran began. By April, 2 months after the war against Iran was launched, China's exports of solar panels were already up by an astonishing 60% compared to the year previously. And by May, their exports of EVs were up by an even more impressive 110% compared with the year previously. By attacking Iran and by being unable to quickly resolve the Hormos situation, the US and Israel have effectively done all of the marketing for China's green energy technology for them. and have turbocharged their sales to never-beforeseen heights in the process. Since the end of the Second World War, the American dollar has been the dominant global reserve currency, used in roughly 80% of international trade finance.
